chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, or someone else, from Aban, from Abu al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When the man establishes the proof upon his right, so there is no swearing of an oath upon him. So if there does not happen to be the proof, so the defendant turns the swearing upon him (the claimant). So if he were to refuse, so there is no right for him.
Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Aban, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
ai.seo_question: What is the rule for oaths in Islamic courts when a claimant lacks proof?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the foundational principle of *bayyinah* (clear proof) in Shia jurisprudence, where the burden of proof lies with the claimant, reflecting the legal maxim 'al-bayyinah 'ala al-muddi''. If the claimant fails to provide evidence, the defendant is given the option to swear an oath (*yamin*) to validate their denial; a refusal to swear is interpreted as an admission of liability, thereby securing the claimant's right. This mechanism underscores the Shia judicial emphasis on balancing evidentiary rigor with the solemnity of oath-taking in the absence of documentary proof.
